source: Li et al. (2023) Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task (Othello-GPT)
finding: A GPT trained only to predict legal Othello moves from move text builds an internal board state. Nonlinear probes find it; linear probes mostly do not. Editing the probed state changes the legal moves the model predicts.
numbers: Illegal-move error rate 0.01% (synthetic data, 20M games) vs 5.17% (championship data, about 140k games) vs 93.29% untrained. Linear probe error never below 20% (synthetic 20.4-23.1%, randomised net about 25%). 2-layer MLP probe error 1.7% best layer (synthetic), 9.4% (championship), 25.5-26.4% randomised.
limits: Probe in a toy closed world with fixed rules. Nonlinear probes can learn the task themselves; the authors use interventions as the causal check. Synthetic data gives a much stronger result than real games.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a state can carry content in the Dretske/Millikan sense (information the consumer uses, causally upstream of output). For our agent: count a representation only if editing it changes behaviour; test with interventions, not readouts.

source: Nanda, Lee, Wattenberg (2023) Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
finding: Re-analysis of Othello-GPT. The board is stored linearly once squares are coded as mine vs yours (relative to the player to move), not black vs white. Linear interventions work as well as the earlier nonlinear ones.
numbers: Probe accuracy: linear black/white/empty about 75%; nonlinear black/white/empty up to 98.7%; linear mine/yours/empty up to 99.6%. Intervention avg errors: 2.723 null vs 0.10 linear add (flip colours); 2.73 null vs 0.02 linear (erase). Removing the flipped-tile feature: 0.486 errors vs 1.686 null.
limits: Resolves the Li et al. linear-probe failure: the coordinate frame was wrong, not the code absent. Still one toy game; probes lose accuracy near game end.
agent_relevance: What a good representation preserves depends on the consumer's frame: self-relative coding was right. When checking whether our agent encodes a state, try frames tied to its own next action.

source: Vafa, Chen, Rambachan, Kleinberg, Mullainathan (2024) Evaluating the World Model Implicit in a Generative Model
finding: Tests whether a sequence model recovers the true state machine using Myhill-Nerode metrics: compression (same state, same continuations) and distinction (different states, different continuations). Models look near perfect on standard tests but fail these.
numbers: NYC taxi transformers: next-token validity 1.00 and state probe 0.91-0.99, yet compression precision 0.10 (shortest paths), 0.05 (noisy shortest), 0.50 (random walks); distinction precision 0.35/0.37/0.99. Valid routes under random detours at 0/1/10/50/75%: shortest-path model 0.99/0.69/0.08/0.00/0.00; random-walk model 0.99/0.99/1.00/0.97/0.74.
limits: Synthetic navigation, Othello and logic puzzles; deterministic automata only. Training distribution decides coherence: random-walk training gave the best model.
agent_relevance: High accuracy on likely inputs does not show content. Test our agent's stored task state by equivalence (two histories, same state, same next moves) and by off-path perturbation.

source: Vafa et al. (2024) Evaluating the World Model Implicit in a Generative Model, Othello and logic-puzzle sections
finding: Same metrics applied to Li et al.'s two Othello models and to prompted LLMs on a seating-arrangement logic puzzle. The Othello model trained on real games fails both metrics; the synthetic-trained one passes. LLMs solve the puzzle yet have incoherent implied states.
numbers: Seating puzzle (3 people): GPT-4 accurate on all fully specified examples; GPT-4 compression 0.21 (SE .04) and distinction 0.56 (.03); GPT-3.5 turbo 1.00 task, compression 0.33, distinction 0.18; Qwen 1.5 110B 0.83 task, 0.53, 0.53. True model 1.00 on all.
quote: models are very capable of solving logic puzzles despite not having a coherent world model
limits: Small puzzle (3 individuals); state defined as the set of consistent seatings. Prompts allowed chain of thought.
agent_relevance: Task success can hide an inconsistent internal state. Our program should hold the state of a problem as a checkable object (set of consistent options), not trust the model's running summary.

source: Mollo & Millière (2023/2025) The Vector Grounding Problem
finding: Philosophical argument using teleosemantics (Millikan, Neander, Shea). Referential grounding needs (1) causal-informational relations to the world and (2) a selection history giving the state the function of carrying that information. They argue LLMs can meet both without senses or a body, via extra-linguistic success conditions such as factuality fine-tuning and preference tuning.
numbers: No experiments. 34 pages. Cites Harnad 1990, Millikan 1989/2017, Neander 1991/2017, Godfrey-Smith 1994, Shea 2018.
quote: referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories
limits: Conceptual; whether training objectives really supply the needed function is contested (they discuss pseudo-learning themselves).
agent_relevance: Gives a criterion that maps to our design: a representation is grounded in our agent when a code-checked outcome selects it. That favours program-checked feedback over model self-grading (G2/G3).

source: Mollo & Millière (2025) The Vector Grounding Problem: preference tuning and pseudo-learning discussion
finding: The paper says helpfulness and factuality tuning can give states a function beyond prediction, but selection that only mimics adaptation is not enough. A state tuned only on rater approval would not be grounded in the facts.
numbers: No experiments.
limits: Whether RLHF raters track the world or just fluency is empirical and unsettled.
agent_relevance: Reason to prefer outcome checks (tests, held-out examples) over model or rater judgement as the selecting signal in our loop.

source: Mandelkern & Linzen (2024) Do Language Models' Words Refer?
finding: Externalist argument (Putnam, Kripke). Reference comes from the natural history of word use, not from the speaker's beliefs or experience, so LM words can refer because the text they train on has causal histories linking it to referents.
numbers: No experiments.
quote: even if the inputs to an LM are simply strings of text, they are strings of text with natural histories
limits: Holds for words with stable usage chains; says little about internal states or reliable use.
agent_relevance: Reference and reliable use are different questions. Bind names to checked objects in code instead of assuming a term the model emits is tied to the task object.

source: Bender & Koller (2020) Climbing towards NLU: On Meaning, Form, and Understanding in the Age of Data
finding: Classic skeptic position: training on form alone cannot in principle yield meaning, since meaning needs a link between form and communicative intent. Introduces the octopus thought experiment.
numbers: No experiments; reviews BERTology evidence that LMs learn formal structure.
quote: We argue that the language modeling task, because it only uses form as training data, cannot in principle lead to learning of meaning.
limits: 2020 position paper; later probing work (Othello-GPT, space and time probes) is the main empirical challenge, and it did not test frontier-scale models.
agent_relevance: The opposing pole to Mollo and Millière. Practical upshot: treat fluent output as form; require grounding through executable checks.

source: Millière & Buckner (2024) A Philosophical Introduction to Language Models Part II: The Way Forward
finding: Reviews interventional interpretability and states the criteria philosophers use to say an activation pattern represents a feature.
numbers: Three criteria: (a) the pattern carries information about the feature; (b) it influences behaviour in a task-relevant way; (c) the model can misrepresent. Reviews probing, nullspace projection (INLP/AlterRep) and causal mediation.
limits: Criterion (c), misrepresentation, is rarely tested in the empirical studies.
agent_relevance: A three-part test we can run on any scaffold state: information, causal use, and a way to be wrong. Our S2 representation should be checked on all three.

source: Gurnee & Tegmark (2024) Language Models Represent Space and Time
finding: Linear probes on Llama-2 7B/13B/70B recover latitude/longitude and dates of entities, with mid-depth layers best. Nonlinear MLP probes add little, so the code is mostly linear.
numbers: Out-of-sample R2 at 60% depth, linear probe, Llama-2-70b: World 0.911, USA 0.864, NYC 0.359, historical figures 0.835, entertainment 0.885, headlines 0.746. 7B linear: 0.881/0.799/0.219/0.785/0.788/0.564. MLP gains at most about 0.02; NYC 70b MLP 0.312 is below linear.
limits: Hold-out tests (whole countries held out) show only weak generalisation: probes partly place items near their country centroid. NYC is weak (R2 0.22-0.36).
agent_relevance: Fine-grained, scale-dependent content exists inside models, but an API-only agent cannot read it; rely on behavioural checks.

source: Gurnee & Tegmark (2024) Language Models Represent Space and Time: robustness and neurons
finding: Probes hold up when entity names are put in different prompts, and probes trained on one entity type (cities) transfer to others (landmarks). Individual space and time neurons are found. Prompts that disturb the entity name hurt, and the period after a headline helps.
numbers: Robustness in Figure 3 for Llama-2-70b across prompt variants; transfer across entity types largely holds with the main loss from block hold-out. No single headline number extracted.
limits: Correlation of a probe with a direction does not show the model uses it; no causal intervention in this paper.
agent_relevance: A same-meaning input in different wording gives the same internal state only mostly; reframing prompts are not free of side effects.

source: Abdou et al. (2021) Can Language Models Encode Perceptual Structure Without Grounding? A Case Study in Color
finding: BERT, RoBERTa, ELECTRA colour-term embeddings align with CIELAB perceptual space by RSA and by linear mapping, and the alignment beats control baselines.
numbers: RSA (Kendall tau) significant in all configurations with only 18 colours; text baselines already nonzero (PMI tau 0.11-0.17, fastText 0.23; linear-mapping selectivity about 0.70-0.72). Shuffled-centroid control gave p > 0.05. Context-controlled condition gave the highest selectivity.
limits: Small sample (18 terms); static text baselines already capture some structure, so the data show structure can come from text, not that it is grounded. Green and blue rank worse.
agent_relevance: The relational structure of a domain can survive in text. For S2: measure representation fidelity against a reference structure, with shuffled controls.

source: Huh, Cheung, Wang, Isola (2024) The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
finding: Representations of different models converge as scale and capability grow. By mutual nearest-neighbour alignment, bigger language models are more similar to bigger vision models.
numbers: 78 vision models compared; language-vision alignment rises roughly linearly with language-model score (1 minus bits per byte). CLIP aligns more, and alignment drops after ImageNet fine-tuning. Absolute alignment values are small (plot axes roughly 0.0-0.2).
quote: representations in AI models, particularly deep networks, are converging
limits: Correlational, metric dependent; authors list counterexamples (no standard representation in robotics; modalities carry non-shared information).
agent_relevance: Weak support for the idea that content is fixed by the world. It does not remove G4: samples from one model family are still correlated.

source: Levinstein & Herrmann (2023) Still No Lie Detector for Language Models
finding: Re-tests supervised truth probes (Azaria & Mitchell) and CCS (Burns et al.) on LLaMA-30B. Probes fail on simple negations and the CCS reconstruction is at chance.
numbers: Supervised probes on negated statements (NegFacts, NegCompanies): accuracy worse than chance in five of six probes. CCS reconstruction accuracy 50% to 57% across runs (chance 50%). Original CCS: often over 80% overall but 62.1% on the one decoder-only model (GPT-J) vs 84.8% for UnifiedQA.
limits: Different prompt format and model than original; later work (Marks & Tegmark) finds better results at larger scale.
agent_relevance: A failed generalisation to negation is the key boundary condition: a truth-like code may track likelihood or topic. Do not rely on model-reported confidence or belief signals as guardrails.

source: Levinstein & Herrmann (2023) Still No Lie Detector: conceptual argument on beliefs
finding: Argues that even if LLMs have beliefs, probes may find other things, and that probes should be checked for expected behaviour over an algebra of propositions closed under negation (footnote 9). Also argues that the arguments claiming LLMs cannot have beliefs are misguided.
numbers: No numbers for this part.
limits: Conceptual; fits a functionalist or interpretationist view of belief.
agent_relevance: A cheap logic check for any claimed representation in our agent: it must respect negation and conjunction, not only match examples.

source: Marks & Tegmark (2024) The Geometry of Truth
finding: Curated true/false datasets show a linear truth direction in LLaMA-2 that grows clearer with scale. Difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalise as well as logistic regression and are more causal when used to steer.
numbers: Truth correlates with text likelihood strongly for cities (r=.85) and sp_en_trans (r=.95), but not for the negated sets. Intervention effects (normalised indirect effect) for mass-mean probes trained on cities+neg_cities: about .13/.19 on 13B vs .55/.99 on 70B (false-to-true / true-to-false). Mass-mean outperforms LR and CCS in causal tests.
limits: Table values read from a flattened PDF, columns may be misaligned. Simple factual statements only; training-set mix matters.
agent_relevance: Scale matters for whether a model holds a generalisable truth code. Small or cheap models in our loop may not.

source: Park, Choe, Veitch (2023) The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
finding: Formalises 'linear representation' three ways (subspace, measurement, intervention) with counterfactual pairs, and links probing to steering through a causal inner product.
numbers: LLaMA-2 experiments on concepts such as language and gender; no headline number extracted.
limits: Only abstract and introduction read; experiments not audited.
agent_relevance: A definition of 'the model represents X' that is testable by both read-out and write-in. Useful to specify operator contracts.

source: Hewitt & Liang (2019) Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks
finding: A probe's high accuracy can reflect probe capacity rather than what the representation contains. Selectivity is task accuracy minus accuracy on a control task with random labels per word type.
numbers: POS tagging, MLP probe: 97.3% task vs 92.8% control, selectivity 4.5. Linear and bilinear probes keep higher selectivity across hyperparameters.
limits: Controls designed for word-level linguistic tasks; board and geometry probes need other controls (Gurnee used hold-outs, Li used interventions).
agent_relevance: Any claim that a trace holds a representation must be shown against a control a memorising probe would also pass.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent World Models and Latent Variable Estimation in Chess-Playing Language Models
finding: A chess GPT trained on real games (character level) stores board state and an estimate of player skill. Adding a skill vector raises win rate.
numbers: Legal move rate 99.8% (16-layer) and 99.6% (8-layer). Win rate vs Stockfish level 0: 46% (8 layers), 64% (16 layers). Best linear probe 99.6% board accuracy. Intervention best success 92%. Skill vector raises win rate up to 2.6 times.
limits: One game, small model; skill finding from one setup.
agent_relevance: Content can include latent variables of the source (skill of the player), not only the world state. S2 may need to keep who or what produced the input.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: Uses the same LLM as an explicit world model (predicts the next state) and as agent, with Monte Carlo tree search over states. A method that makes the state representation explicit inside an agent loop.
numbers: Blocksworld success on 2/4/6-step: CoT (LLaMA-33B) 0.17/0.02/0.00; CoT pass@10 0.23/0.07/0.00; CoT (GPT-4) 0.50/0.63/0.40; RAP(10) 1.00/0.86/0.26; RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42. GSM8k RAP 48.8%. ProofWriter answer accuracy 94.2%, proof accuracy 78.8%.
limits: Base model LLaMA-33B vs GPT-4 CoT mismatched; GPT-4 CoT beats RAP(10) at 6 steps. Cost rises with iterations.
agent_relevance: Closest pattern to our S2: write the state explicitly at each step. Helps weaker models, but the state must be checked by code (see Wang et al.).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Can Language Models Serve as Text-Based World Simulators?
finding: GPT-4 asked to predict the next state of a text game is often wrong, especially for environment-driven changes.
numbers: Best case GPT-4 simulates 77.1% of dynamic action-driven transitions and at most 49.7% of environment-driven ones. Game-progress prediction 92.1% with rules in context, 61.5% without. Human accuracy 80% vs sampled LLM 50% on one comparison. Dataset 2954 transition tuples.
limits: One model family (GPT-4), text-game domain, no later models.
agent_relevance: The state our agent writes can drift from the true state. Do not let the model be its own simulator; code should apply transitions.

source: Mancoridis, Vafa, Weeks, Mullainathan (2025) Potemkin Understanding in Large Language Models
finding: Models define concepts correctly yet fail to use them. A correct definition does not guarantee a working representation for classify, generate or edit tasks.
numbers: Definitions correct 94.2% of the time. Potemkin rate (error given a correct definition; classification rescaled so chance = 1), overall 0.55 (SE .02) / 0.40 (.03) / 0.40 (.02) for the three use tasks. GPT-4o 0.53/0.38/0.35; Claude-3.5 0.49/0.23/0.29; DeepSeek-R1 0.47/0.39/0.52; Qwen2-VL 0.66/0.62/0.52. 224 and 791 annotated responses for two tasks.
limits: Three domains (literary technique, game theory, psychological biases); column order read as classify, generate, edit.
agent_relevance: For S2: a correct restatement of the problem may not be used correctly. Check by using the representation, not reading it.

source: Mancoridis et al. (2025) Potemkin Understanding: incoherence and lower-bound procedure
finding: A general automated test: the model answers an MMLU question, writes related questions, answers them, then grades itself. Self-disagreement shows incoherence. Even this lower bound is high.
numbers: Lower-bound potemkin rate on MMLU-derived questions: 0.62 (scaled so 1 = chance, 0 = perfect). A slightly wrong decoy response is added to guard against judge sycophancy.
limits: Uses the same model as grader, so it is a lower bound; judge errors can hide misunderstanding.
agent_relevance: A cheap self-consistency probe the program can run without human labels, but the grader is a model so it only supplies a flag, not proof (G3).

source: Slocum et al. (2025) Believe It or Not: How Deeply Do LLMs Believe Implanted Facts?
finding: Defines belief depth by generalisation, robustness to scrutiny and probe similarity to true knowledge. Synthetic document fine-tuning implants deep beliefs; prompting and mechanistic editing do not. Facts that contradict basic world knowledge stay brittle.
numbers: Abstract-level results only; per-method percentages not extracted.
limits: Only abstract and introduction examined this session.
agent_relevance: A behavioural test battery for 'does the model really represent X', usable as a template for checking facts injected by the scaffold.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Mental Representation (Pitt)
finding: Maps the classic theories: Fodor's asymmetric dependency theory and teleological theories (Dretske 1988/1995, Millikan 1984, Neander, Papineau). Core problem: separating informational from representational relations and allowing misrepresentation.
numbers: Reference entry; no experiments.
limits: Searched for theory names, not read cover to cover.
agent_relevance: The disjunction problem (what makes a state wrong rather than about something else) matters for judging agent state: define content by what the consumer uses it for.
